# robots.txt rules

A crawler obeys only the most specific group that names it; within the group the longest matching path wins, and ties go to the less restrictive rule. An audio recording of Google's Day 1 robots.txt talk added the history and the basics. Robots.txt began in 1994, when Martijn Koster proposed a text file of access rules because bots were crashing servers; Google has supported it since it started crawling in 1996, and it is now an IETF standard, RFC 9309, the Robots Exclusion Protocol, which Google follows because anyone who wants to opt out of crawling should be able to. Google stressed that the protocol only controls which automated clients may access what, not how the content is used, and that it is not a security measure: the file always sits at the root of the host, where anyone can read the paths it disallows, so a secret folder needs authentication. Everything is implicitly allowed, so an allow rule only re-opens a path inside a disallowed one; * matches any characters and $ ends the match, so user-agent: *, disallow: / and allow: /$ let unnamed crawlers fetch only the homepage. Comments start with #, and the talk pointed to the ASCII-art robots.txt of thebestfriedchickenever.com to show why they are useful. Google called the format extremely forgiving: lines a parser cannot read are skipped, a typo in a path blocks only the wrong path and a misspelt rule name makes Google ignore that line (not in Google's docs). Search Console's robots.txt report shows the file as Google last fetched it, with a version history and the errors and successes of each fetch; Google said the report uses its open-source parser and helps catch CDNs that change robots.txt without the owner knowing and hosts that cloak the file, which happens more often than people think (not in Google's docs). In Lightning session B Dave Smart added that robots.txt is checked for every URL in a redirect chain and crawling stops at the first blocked one: a page that redirected through a disallowed /cart/ URL to set the local currency was reported as blocked, and Search Console names only the first URL of the chain, which is not itself disallowed; the same happens with an external authorisation service blocked by its own robots.txt, content that moved through several URLs and redirects served only to Googlebot (the per-URL check is not in Google's docs). Google supports only user-agent, allow, disallow and sitemap, and Day 2 confirmed that a sitemap line can be picked up by any crawler, while a sitemap not listed there has to be submitted, for example in Search Console. A disallow is not a noindex: Google does not index a disallowed page's content, but its URL can still appear in results. Google said it will not treat a disallow as noindex because some very important sites block their most important pages by accident (said at the event, not in Google's docs). Day 2 also showed that disallowing JavaScript or API endpoints a page needs for rendering leaves its content missing, and that rules apply per host, so an API or CDN on its own hostname has its own robots.txt. Day 3 added timing and Shopping: Google said its service level objective is to refresh robots.txt every 24 hours, as RFC 9309 calls for and its robots.txt guide confirms, though delays happen, and that requesting a recrawl in Search Console's robots.txt report refreshes it sooner. Rules addressed to Storebot-Google affect all Google Shopping surfaces, such as the Shopping tab. The second recordings added Google's own stance. Gary Illyes said all of Google's automated crawlers obey robots.txt, which Google treats as the way site owners opt out of its crawling, except contractual crawlers that crawl by agreement; on Day 2 Google repeated that site owners should be able to opt out, for legal reasons or for crawl budget, and in the Day 1 Q&A said it follows robots.txt partly in its own interest, since crawling a blocked infinite URL space would waste its time too. Mainstream crawlers from search engines and AI companies try to follow robots.txt, so correct rules are the control; user-initiated fetchers and agents acting for a user generally do not check it, and a panelist noted that much of robots.txt is written for search engines, which should never add items to a cart, while an agent probably should. A panelist also mentioned crawler best practices in progress that would exempt research, malware-scanning and privacy crawlers, apparently because they sometimes need to ignore robots.txt or probe URLs other crawlers would not touch. Day 2's opening Q&A said listing a sitemap in robots.txt is fine but makes the sitemap public, and explained why a disallow is not a noindex with a national tax authority that blocks very important PDFs: Google can show their URLs but cannot index their content; very few disallowed URLs are in the index, and John Mueller added that robots meta rules only work if robots.txt lets Google fetch the page. For media, rules for Googlebot-Image and Googlebot-Video control image and video indexing, and a video blocked by robots.txt is not shown by its bare URL at all (said at the event, not in Google's docs). Author's view: the best practices mentioned match the public IETF draft 'Crawler best practices', not Google documentation; and Google's docs name links from elsewhere as the reason a disallowed URL can still be indexed, so keep an important page crawlable with noindex if it must stay out of Search. Author's view: Google's open-source parser in fact accepts common misspellings of disallow and user-agent, though not of allow, and other crawlers may be stricter, so spell rule names correctly.

## What to do

- Never disallow JavaScript, CSS or API endpoints that rendering needs; if an API folder must stay blocked, allow only what rendering uses (for example Disallow: /api/ with Allow: /api/products/).
- To keep a page out of Search, allow crawling and use noindex; a disallow alone can leave the bare URL in results.
- Test each important URL pattern against the group that applies to each crawler, for Google with its open-source robots.txt parser.
- Check robots.txt on every host a page loads data from, including API and CDN subdomains.
- List your XML sitemaps in robots.txt so every crawler can find them.
- Check that the homepage with tracking parameters is not blocked by an 'allow /$' pattern.
- Plan robots.txt changes a day ahead, and request a refresh in Search Console when a change is urgent.
- Leave a sitemap out of robots.txt if you do not want it public, and submit it in Search Console instead.
- Use Googlebot-Image and Googlebot-Video groups, or disallow the file locations, to control which images and videos Google indexes.
- Protect private paths with authentication, not robots.txt: anyone can read the file and the paths it disallows.
- Use allow rules only to re-open a path inside a disallowed one; everything else is allowed by default.
- When Search Console reports a URL as blocked by robots.txt that the file does not block, test every URL in its redirect chain.
- Check the version history in Search Console's robots.txt report after CDN or hosting changes, to catch rule changes you did not make.
- Spell rule names correctly: Google ignores or tolerates some typos, but other crawlers may be stricter.

- **[Stage]** Mainstream crawlers from Google, other large search engines and AI companies try to follow robots.txt, so implementing robots.txt correctly is the way to stop them doing something specific on a site.
  <br><sub>`D1-C428` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · confirmed by Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro), [Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/overview-google-crawlers) · Answers [D1-C427](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A Google panelist said crawlers that ignore robots.txt and cause a nuisance are better treated as a scraping problem than as a crawling problem.
  <br><sub>`D1-C429` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · Answers [D1-C427](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google follows robots.txt partly in its own interest: crawling an infinite URL space such as a calendar that robots.txt blocks would waste Google's crawling time as well as the site's resources.
  <br><sub>`D1-C430` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Used by `DEV-URL-08`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A Google panelist described research, malware-scanning and privacy crawlers as a separate category of crawler that is generally harmless and useful to the web.
  <br><sub>`D1-C431` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A Google panelist said they were working on a set of crawler best practices and offering research, malware-scanning and privacy crawlers an exemption from following them, apparently because such crawlers sometimes need to ignore robots.txt or probe URLs that other crawlers would not touch (the reason is a best reading: the audio has 'don't need', which would not explain an exemption).
  <br><sub>`D1-C432` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D1-C433](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** User-initiated fetchers, such as a translation service fetching a page a user asked to translate, are a different category from crawlers and generally do not check robots.txt, because a user asked for the fetch.
  <br><sub>`D1-C434` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · confirmed by Google docs · [List of Google user-triggered fetchers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-user-triggered-fetchers) · Repeats [D1-C273](../sessions/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) · Extended by [D2-C122](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-05`, the glossary term *User-triggered fetchers*</sub>

- **[Stage]** A Google panelist said much of robots.txt is written with search engines in mind: a search engine should never add items to a cart or check out, but an agent acting for a user probably should be able to.
  <br><sub>`D1-C437` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said disallowing a section that should not be crawled, such as /ads, in a Googlebot group in robots.txt shifts crawl budget to the rest of the site.
  <br><sub>`D1-C469` · Day 1, Q&A (Gary Illyes) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Answers [D1-C465](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Extended by [D1-C470](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-08`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Nearly all mainstream AI crawlers and AI systems use their own user agents, so robots.txt can set a separate policy for each; at the event OpenAI was said to have three or four, Anthropic a few and Microsoft some.
  <br><sub>`D1-C482` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · consistent with Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Answers [D1-C481](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Extended by [D2-C067](../sessions/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** When logs show an unknown crawler fetching a lot, search for its user agent online to find the robots.txt token that controls it; the mainstream crawlers that send the most traffic can all be controlled this way.
  <br><sub>`D1-C488` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Answers [D1-C481](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A Google panelist called a default-deny robots.txt, which blocks every crawler and allows only chosen ones, a bad pattern because the site owner does not know what is being blocked.
  > "Personally, I think that's a bad pattern, because you don't know what you're blocking."
  <br><sub>`D1-C489` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · Answers [D1-C481](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-05`</sub>

- **[Slide]** An audience member asked whether the sitemap link should be included in robots.txt, noting that many websites include it but that it was missing from an earlier robots.txt slide by a Google speaker, which the question called 'Gary's slide'.
  <br><sub>`D2-C015` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (audience member) · Answered by [D2-C017](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C018](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C842](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C843](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md)</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that a sitemap listed in the robots.txt file can be picked up by any crawler, not only by Google's.
  > "If it's included in the robots.txt file, any crawler can pick your sitemaps up"
  <br><sub>`D2-C017` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Answers [D2-C015](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D1-C084](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extends [D1-C079](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D2-C843](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-05`</sub>

- **[Slide]** An audience member noted that a robots.txt block does not mean noindex and that explaining this to developers is a constant struggle, and asked why Google does not treat a robots.txt block as a noindex.
  <br><sub>`D2-C019` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (audience member) · Answered by [D2-C020](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C021](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C844](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C845](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Answered by [D2-C846](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md)</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as a noindex because some extremely important sites disallow their most important pages, by accident or out of ignorance.
  > "Simply put, it's because of sites that are extremely important and like to disallow their most important pages, either accidentally or out of ignorance."
  <br><sub>`D2-C020` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · not in Google docs · Answers [D2-C019](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D1-C110](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extended by [D2-C844](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google's Q&A slide said Google does not index the content of pages disallowed in robots.txt, but users will still find the URLs of those pages in Search.
  <br><sub>`D2-C021` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro), [No page information in search results](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7489871?hl=en) · Answers [D2-C019](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D1-C105](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extended by [D2-C846](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Repeated by [D2-C851](../sessions/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Extended by [D2-C933](../sessions/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google illustrated why it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as noindex with an extremely important site, such as a national tax authority, that blocks very important PDF files with robots.txt: Google cannot index the PDFs' content but can at least show their URLs in search results.
  <br><sub>`D2-C844` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) · Answers [D2-C019](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D2-C020](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said a URL disallowed by robots.txt might still be indexed if the URL is important, in which case the URL is indexed but not its content.
  > "if a URL is important, then it might get indexed even if it's disallowed by robots.txt. So the URL gets indexed, not the content."
  <br><sub>`D2-C846` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · consistent with Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) · Answers [D2-C019](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D2-C021](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D1-C110](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said it strongly believes site owners should be able to opt out of crawling and control how their site is crawled, which can matter for legal reasons or for crawl budget.
  <br><sub>`D2-C848` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · consistent with Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro), [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Repeats [D1-C329](../sessions/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** John Mueller noted that robots.txt is defined by an internet standard, RFC 9309, which Google's Gary Illyes co-authored.

- **[Stage]** John Mueller said robots meta rules only work if robots.txt allows Google to fetch the page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C850` · Day 2, Controlling indexing (John Mueller) · confirmed by Google docs · [Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag), [Block Search indexing with noindex](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/block-indexing) · Repeats [D1-C110](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** When robots.txt blocks a page, the page's content is not indexable but Google can still index its URL, John Mueller said.
  <br><sub>`D2-C851` · Day 2, Controlling indexing (John Mueller) · confirmed by Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro), [Block Search indexing with noindex](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/block-indexing) · Repeats [D2-C021](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Repeats [D1-C110](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Never block a resource that a page needs for rendering with robots.txt, a community speaker said, calling this common sense.
  <br><sub>`D2-C157` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Sören Bendig) · confirmed by Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro), [Crawling December: The how and why of Googlebot crawling](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/12/crawling-december-resources), [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics)</sub>

- **[Stage]** For each suspect script or API request in Chrome DevTools, check whether it runs, whether something blocks it and whether robots.txt disallows it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C181` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · consistent with Google docs · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics), [Fix Search-related JavaScript problems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript)</sub>

- **[Slide]** Blocking JavaScript or API resources in robots.txt is a classic rendering mistake: if Google's renderer cannot fetch a resource, it cannot run it.
  > "If the renderer can't fetch it, the renderer can't run it."
  <br><sub>`D2-C204` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · confirmed by Google docs · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics), [Crawling December: The how and why of Googlebot crawling](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/12/crawling-december-resources), [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) · Extends [D1-C064](../sessions/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) · Repeated by [D2-C265](../sessions/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) · Repeated by [D2-C296](../sessions/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-04`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Disallowing a script folder such as /static/js/ or a generic /api/ folder in robots.txt can block the endpoints that supply a page's content, leaving blank modules and missing content after rendering.
  <br><sub>`D2-C205` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · consistent with Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro), [Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post), [Crawling December: The how and why of Googlebot crawling](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/12/crawling-december-resources)</sub>

- **[Slide]** If an API folder must stay blocked in robots.txt, allow the endpoints that rendering needs, for example Disallow: /api/ together with Allow: /api/products/.
  > "Carve out only what rendering needs."
  <br><sub>`D2-C207` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · consistent with Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec), [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) · Used by `DEV-REN-04`</sub>

- **[Slide]** robots.txt rules apply per host, so the rules in example.com/robots.txt do not apply at all to an API served from api.example.com.
  <br><sub>`D2-C209` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · confirmed by Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Used by `DEV-SRV-04`, the glossary term *robots.txt*</sub>

- **[Slide]** Blocked resources, one of Google's four common JavaScript indexing problems, means robots.txt disallowing the crawling of critical JavaScript files or API endpoints.
  > "robots.txt disallowing crawling of critical .js or API endpoints."
  <br><sub>`D2-C265` · Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · consistent with Google docs · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics), [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) · Repeats [D2-C204](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-04`</sub>

- **[Stage]** If robots.txt blocks JavaScript that client-side code needs to render, Google cannot render the content that the JavaScript would produce.
  <br><sub>`D2-C296` · Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · confirmed by Google docs · [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics) · Extends [D1-C064](../sessions/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) · Repeats [D2-C204](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-04`</sub>

- **[Stage]** The canonical leader of a group should be indexable: it should carry no noindex robots directive, return no error status code and not be blocked in robots.txt.
  <br><sub>`D2-C432` · Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves (Tobias Schwarz) · consistent with Google docs · [5 common mistakes with rel=canonical](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2013/04/5-common-mistakes-with-relcanonical), [How to specify a canonical URL with rel="canonical" and other methods](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) · Used by `DEV-CAN-04`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Googlebot-Image and Googlebot-Video are the Google crawlers that fetch images and videos, and robots.txt rules addressed to their user agent tokens control how Google indexes a site's images and videos.
  <br><sub>`D2-C931` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [List of Google's common crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-common-crawlers) · Used by `DEV-IMG-06`, the glossary term *Googlebot-Image and Googlebot-Video*</sub>

- **[Stage]** If robots.txt disallows the location of an image or video file, Google does not index that image or video.
  <br><sub>`D2-C932` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [Remove images hosted on your site from search results](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/prevent-images-on-your-page), [Video SEO best practices](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/video) · Used by `DEV-IMG-06`, `DEV-VID-06`, the glossary term *Googlebot-Image and Googlebot-Video*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Unlike a disallowed web page, whose bare URL can still appear in web results, a video blocked by robots.txt is not shown by its URL, because Google sees no good reason to show a video URL alone.
  <br><sub>`D2-C933` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C021](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-VID-06`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google estimated that a robots.txt update is picked up in about 24 hours, with a minimum of seconds and an end point of 25 hours on the slide.
  <br><sub>`D3-C613` · Day 3, How long does it take to..? (Gary Illyes, Search Relations) · confirmed by Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec), [Update your robots.txt file](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/submit-updated-robots-txt) · Extends [D1-C085](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-10`, `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said its service level objective is to refresh robots.txt every 24 hours, as RFC 9309 calls for, though delays happen now and then.
  <br><sub>`D3-C614` · Day 3, How long does it take to..? (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec), [Update your robots.txt file](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/submit-updated-robots-txt) · Extends [D1-C085](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A site owner can submit robots.txt in Search Console to force Google to refresh it sooner.
  <br><sub>`D3-C615` · Day 3, How long does it take to..? (Gary Illyes) · confirmed by Google docs · [Update your robots.txt file](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/submit-updated-robots-txt), [robots.txt report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/6062598) · Extends [D1-C140](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

## What Google's documentation says

- **[Docs]** Google's crawler documentation says special-case crawlers serve specific Google products where the crawled site and the product have an agreement about the crawl process, so they may ignore robots.txt rules; AdsBot, for example, ignores the global (*) user agent with the ad publisher's permission.
  <br><sub>`D1-C343` · Google · annotates Day 1, How crawling works · is the documentation · [List of Google's special-case crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-special-case-crawlers), [Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/overview-google-crawlers) · Used by the glossary term *Contractual crawlers (special-case crawlers)*</sub>

- **[Docs]** If robots.txt returns a 5xx error, Google stops crawling the site for the first 12 hours, then uses the cached copy for up to 30 days.
  <br><sub>`D1-C074` · Google · annotates Day 1, How crawling errors affect Search · is the documentation · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D2-C210](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-04`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Rules can be grouped for several crawlers by repeating user-agent lines. A crawler follows only the most specific group that names it.
  <br><sub>`D1-C080` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D1-C519](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D1-C527](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D1-C531](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D1-C533](../sessions/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`, `DEV-SRV-10`, the glossary term *User-agent group*</sub>

- **[Docs]** When matching rules to a URL, Google uses the most specific rule by path length. If rules conflict, it uses the least restrictive one.
  > "In case of conflicting rules, including those with wildcards, Google uses the least restrictive rule."
  <br><sub>`D1-C081` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D1-C520](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D2-C208](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** In robots.txt, * matches zero or more of any character and $ marks the end of the URL.
  <br><sub>`D1-C082` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D1-C521](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google supports only the user-agent, allow, disallow and sitemap fields in robots.txt. Other fields such as crawl-delay are not supported.
  <br><sub>`D1-C084` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D1-C516](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D2-C017](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extended by [D2-C842](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`, the glossary term *robots.txt*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google generally caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours and reads only the first 500 KiB of the file.
  <br><sub>`D1-C085` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D3-C613](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Extended by [D3-C614](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt files Google found for the top 20 hosts of a Domain property, with their fetch status, warnings and errors; to test whether a specific URL is blocked, Google's help page points to the URL Inspection tool and to Google's open-source robots.txt library.
  <br><sub>`D1-C140` · Google Search Console Help · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [robots.txt report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/6062598) · Extended by [D1-C528](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D1-C530](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D3-C615](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's noindex documentation says the noindex rule works only if the page is not blocked by robots.txt: a crawler that cannot fetch the page never sees the rule, and the page can still appear in search results, for example if other pages link to it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C022` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · is the documentation · [Block Search indexing with noindex](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/block-indexing) · Extends [D1-C106](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`, the glossary term *noindex*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's robots meta tag specification says robots meta tags and X-Robots-Tag headers are found only when a URL is crawled, so the rules on a URL disallowed in robots.txt are never seen and are ignored.
  <br><sub>`D2-C069` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing · is the documentation · [Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag), [Block Search indexing with noindex](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/block-indexing) · Extends [D1-C106](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`, `DEV-IDX-03`, the glossary term *X-Robots-Tag*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google says user-triggered fetchers, which fetch a URL because a user asked for it in a Google product (for example Gemini Notebook fetching URLs users add as sources, or Google-Agent acting on a user's request), generally ignore robots.txt rules.
  <br><sub>`D2-C122` · Google · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · is the documentation · [List of Google user-triggered fetchers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-user-triggered-fetchers) · Repeats [D1-C273](../sessions/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) · Extends [D1-C434](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-11`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's introduction to robots.txt says unimportant image, script or style files may be blocked, but resources whose absence makes a page harder for Google to understand should not be blocked.
  <br><sub>`D2-C297` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript · is the documentation · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) · Used by `DEV-REN-04`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's crawler list says robots.txt rules addressed to the Storebot-Google user agent affect all surfaces of Google Shopping, such as the Shopping tab in Google Search.
  <br><sub>`D3-C389` · Google · annotates Day 3, Shopping on Search: Beyond the blue links · is the documentation · [List of Google's common crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-common-crawlers) · Used by `DEV-SHP-02`, the glossary term *Storebot-Google*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's robots.txt guide says its crawlers update their cached copy of a site's robots.txt every 24 hours, and that the Request a recrawl option in Search Console's robots.txt report refreshes it faster.
  <br><sub>`D3-C667` · Google Search Central, Google Search Console Help · annotates Day 3, How long does it take to..? · is the documentation · [Update your robots.txt file](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/submit-updated-robots-txt), [robots.txt report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/6062598) · Extends [D1-C528](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

## Analysis

- **[Analysis]** Under the example file, Googlebot may crawl /, /politics/eu-vote and /sports/live/, and is blocked from /?utm_source=x, /index.html, /politics (no trailing slash), /live/ and /sports/live-score. An 'allow: /$' rule does not cover the homepage with tracking parameters.
  <br><sub>`D1-C083` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt</sub>

- **[Analysis]** A typo in a rule name is not always ignored by Google: its open-source robots.txt parser deliberately accepts common misspellings of disallow (such as dissallow, dissalow and disalow) and of user-agent (useragent, user agent), but not of allow. Google's spec page does not mention typos, and other crawlers may be stricter, so spell rule names correctly.
  <br><sub>`D1-C532` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · [google/robotstxt](https://github.com/google/robotstxt), [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extends [D1-C525](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The crawler best practices mentioned on stage match the public IETF Internet-Draft 'Crawler best practices' (draft-illyes-aipref-cbcp-00, July 2025), which says self-declared research crawlers, including privacy and malware discovery crawlers, may exempt themselves from any of its practices with a rationale; it is a draft, not Google documentation.
  <br><sub>`D1-C433` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, Q&A · Extends [D1-C432](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Explain robots.txt and noindex to developers as two separate controls: robots.txt controls crawling, noindex controls indexing. To keep a page out of Search, let Google crawl it and serve noindex; a robots.txt disallow alone can leave the bare URL in results.
  <br><sub>`D2-C023` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Google's robots.txt introduction names links from elsewhere on the web as the reason a disallowed URL can still be indexed, while on stage Google spoke of the URL's importance; either way, well-linked important URLs are the disallowed ones most likely to appear in results, so keep such pages crawlable with noindex if they must stay out of Search.
  <br><sub>`D2-C849` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · Extends [D1-C110](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** When something is missing from a rendered page, check both robots.txt and the Content Security Policy: the URL Inspection live test shows the page resources, the JavaScript console output and a screenshot of the rendered page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C158` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Used by `DEV-MON-02`, `DEV-REN-09`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** A robots.txt carve-out works because Google applies the most specific matching rule, so Allow: /api/products/ beats Disallow: /api/ for product endpoints only; re-test a rendered page after every robots.txt change to script or API paths.
  <br><sub>`D2-C208` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Extends [D1-C081](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** An API or CDN on its own host needs its own robots.txt check: a blanket Disallow there, or a robots.txt that returns 5xx errors, can stop Google fetching the data a page renders from.
  <br><sub>`D2-C210` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Extends [D1-C074](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-04`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Make sure robots.txt does not block the URLs from which the browser loads a fragment's assets (the gateway paths on the host page's origin, or the endpoint's own host if assets load from there), because Google does not render JavaScript from blocked files and robots.txt rules apply per host.
  <br><sub>`D2-C245` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec), [Understand the JavaScript SEO basics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Check robots.txt for Disallow rules covering JavaScript bundles, build folders or API endpoints the page calls while rendering, including on separate API or CDN hostnames with their own robots.txt, then confirm in URL Inspection's live test that the rendered HTML contains the main content.
  <br><sub>`D2-C298` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Treat Storebot-Google separately from Googlebot in robots.txt and bot protection: a shop that blocks it on product, cart or checkout paths can undermine Shopping price and availability checks, even when Googlebot is allowed.
  <br><sub>`D3-C390` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Shopping on Search: Beyond the blue links · Used by `DEV-SHP-02`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Plan robots.txt changes a day ahead, because Google may use the old file for about 24 hours; for an urgent change, request a refresh in Search Console instead of waiting.
  <br><sub>`D3-C616` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, How long does it take to..? · [Update your robots.txt file](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/submit-updated-robots-txt)</sub>

## Built on these claims

The items of the developer and content kits that rest on this topic's claims.

- Requirement `DEV-AIF-05`: Set robots.txt policy per AI crawler by its own token, and know that user-triggered fetchers ignore it
- Requirement `DEV-CAN-04`: Point every canonical directly at a final URL that returns 200, is indexable and is linked
- Requirement `DEV-CAN-11`: Never route a crawlable URL's redirects through a URL that robots.txt blocks
- Requirement `DEV-IDX-01`: Use noindex to keep a page out of Search, and leave that URL crawlable
- Requirement `DEV-IDX-02`: Do not use noindex, nofollow or crawl-delay to save crawl budget
- Requirement `DEV-IDX-03`: Send robots rules for PDFs, images and other non-HTML files in the X-Robots-Tag header
- Requirement `DEV-IDX-11`: Use the Google-Extended robots.txt token to control Gemini training and grounding
- Requirement `DEV-IMG-06`: Keep images out of Search with robots.txt or X-Robots-Tag, not with CSS tricks
- Requirement `DEV-MON-02`: Render every template in a headless browser before release and check it in URL Inspection right after
- Requirement `DEV-MON-10`: Plan releases and fixes around Google's processing times, and judge results only after them
- Requirement `DEV-REN-04`: Do not block JavaScript, CSS or API endpoints that pages need for rendering in robots.txt
- Requirement `DEV-REN-09`: Monitor JavaScript console errors and Content Security Policy violations on key templates
- Requirement `DEV-SHP-02`: Let Storebot-Google crawl product, cart and checkout pages, through robots.txt and bot protection
- Requirement `DEV-SRV-04`: Keep robots.txt reachable on every host: 200 with rules, or 404 if there are none
- Requirement `DEV-SRV-05`: Rely only on the fields Google supports (user-agent, allow, disallow, sitemap) and keep robots.txt under 500 KiB
- Requirement `DEV-SRV-06`: Do not put Content-Signal or other non-standard lines between user-agent lines
- Requirement `DEV-SRV-10`: Give a crawler its own robots.txt group only when needed, and make that group complete
- Requirement `DEV-SRV-11`: Never use robots.txt to hide private paths; protect them with authentication
- Requirement `DEV-URL-05`: Publish XML sitemaps listing only canonical, indexable URLs with accurate lastmod
- Requirement `DEV-URL-08`: Keep faceted navigation out of the crawl with robots.txt rules or URL fragments
- Requirement `DEV-VID-06`: Serve videos fast in a common container with standard codecs, and never block the files
- Fact `F-025`: noindex costs crawl budget because Google must fetch a page to see the rule, while URLs disallowed in robots.txt are not fetched at all.
- Glossary term *Contractual crawlers (special-case crawlers)*
- Glossary term *Googlebot-Image and Googlebot-Video*
- Glossary term *noindex*
- Glossary term *Redirect chain*
- Glossary term *RFC 9309 (Robots Exclusion Protocol)*
- Glossary term *robots.txt*
- Glossary term *robots.txt report*
- Glossary term *Storebot-Google*
